description.p: LACTAMS

The present invention relates to lactams, processes for their preparation and their use as inhibitors of enzymes comprising a nucleophilic serine or cysteine residue at their active sites. The invention in particular relates to monocyclic γ-lactams or larger ring lactams and their use, for example, as inhibitors of serine proteases such as elastase, thrombin, trypsin and chymotrypsin or as antibiotics. β-Lactam antibiotics are known to exert their biological activity by acylation of nucleophilic serinyl residues at the active site of penicillin binding proteins (PBPs), or transpeptidase enzymes, thus inhibiting the cross-linking of bacterial cell walls. β-Lactams have also been shown to inhibit a range of other enzymes with nucleophilic residues at their active sites, including serine proteases.

The inhibition of elastases by β-lactams has been studied in detail. It is known that an initial reaction occurs to form an acyl-enzyme ester complex which then partitions between a conformational change to form a long lived enzyme- inhibitor complex or hydrolysis to give a β-amino acid as shown in Scheme 1. The proposed mechanism involves nucleophilic attack of the oxygen of the serine residue on the carbonyl carbon of the β-lactam. The release of ca. 25 kcal of ring strain energy during ring opening of a β-lactam by a hydroxyl group renders reformation of the β-lactam energetically unfavourable. The nature of the conformational change which results in a long lived enzyme-inhibitor complex has also been studied. It is proposed that the β-lactam initially reacts to form a hydrolytically labile covalent acyl-enzyme complex in which the ester carbonyl is located within an oxyanion hole. Rotation of the ester carbonyl out of the oxyanion hole and displacement of, for example, hydrolytic water gives rise to a hydrolytically stable complex.

β-Lactams antibiotics are, however, susceptible to degradation by β-lactamase enzymes which neutralise many clinically useful antibiotics by cleaving the β-lactam ring. Many bacteria contain β-lactamases and are therefore resistant to β-lactam antibiotics. Thus efforts have been made to find alternatives to β-lactam compounds.
The present invention provides monocyclic γ-lactams and larger ring lactams which may be more stable than β-lactams as they may be less susceptible to decomposition mediated by resistance mechanisms.

It will be appreciated that R1 is selected to stabilise the acyl-enzyme complex formed between the compound of formula (I) and the enzyme which is to be inhibited. Stabilisation may be achieved by, for example, choosing an R1 group which reduces or eliminates the availability of the nitrogen lone pair for attack onto the carbonyl of the acyl-enzyme complex by mesomeric or resonance effects. Accordingly R1 is typically hydrogen, SO2R7, CO2R7, CONHR7, COR7, C=CR8R9 wherein R7 is Ci to C6 alkyl; CH2(CF2)0.4CF3; aryl or heteroaryl, which aryl or heteroaryl are mono-ring, or have two fused rings one of which may be saturated, and which aryl and heteroaryl groups may be substituted by one or more Cj to C4 alkyl, halo, NR10Rn, SO2R10 R11, CONR10Rn, C, to C6 alkyl ester, CN, CH2OH, O- to C6 alkyl, CF3 or nitro groups; aryl-Cj to C4 alkyl; aryl- to C4-alkyl-NH; or aryl-C2 to C4 alkenyl; or such groups wherein aryl is substituted by one or more to C4 alkyl or halo groups; R8 and R9, which may be the same or different, are COR12; R10 and
R11, which may be the same or different, are hydrogen or C, to C4 alkyl; and R12 is hydrogen or an aliphatic, aromatic or heteroaromatic group.

R2 and R3 are selected to enhance productive binding and formation of the acyl-enzyme complex. When X1 is CR2R3 the groups R2 and R3 may be important in positioning the lactam in the active site of the enzyme. In the case of enzymes such as elastase, thrombin, trypsin and chymotrypsin when X1 is CR2R3 the groups R2 and R3 can bind into the SI pocket of the enzyme and should be selected to do so. Suitable R2 and R3 groups include ethyl, propyl, isopropyl, butyl, isobutyl, methoxy, ethoxy, propoxy, methylthio, ethylthio, propylthio, basic groups such as amino, amidino and guanidino, benzyl, phenyl, C6H5CH2CONH and C6H5OCH2CONH.

R5 is selected to enhance hydrogen bonding and stability within the acyl- enzyme complex. In the case of, for example, elastase R5 may be chosen to stabilise the acyl-enzyme complex by displacement of the histidine of the catalytic triad from its catalytic position or to make favourable hydrogen bonds with the NH group of the valine 216 or the C=O group of the serine 214. The R5 group may be, for example

CO2R12, CONHR12, NHCOR12, NHSO2R12, OCOR12 or OCONHR12 wherein R12 is as
defined above. R5 may also be chosen so as to displace the hydrolytic water (i.e. the water molecule positioned within the active site to effect hydrolysis of the acyl- enzyme complex).

The present invention also includes the salts of those compounds of formula (I) that have salt forming groups, such as an acidic or basic group. The^salts are physiologically tolerable salts. In the case of compounds comprising a basic amino group, the salts are formed with suitable inorganic or organic acids. Inorganic acids are, for example, hydrochloric or sulphuric acid. Suitable organic acids include mono-, di- and tricarboxylic acids, such as acetic, trifluoroacetic, tartaric and citric acid, or sulphonic acids, for example methanesulphonic, trifluoromethanesulphonic or/?-toluenesulphonic acid.

The present invention includes all possible isomers and mixtures thereof, including diastereomeric mixtures and racemic mixtures, resulting from the possible combinations of (R) and (S) stereochemistry. In another aspect the present invention provides non-therapeutic use, for
example in an assay, of the compounds of formula (I) as inhibitors of enzymes such as elastases, thrombin, factor Xa, trypsin, chymotrypsin, transpeptidase enzymes or β-lactamases.

In a further aspect the present invention provides a pharmaceutical composition comprising a compound of formula (I) or a pharmaceutically acceptable salt thereof, as active ingredient, in association with a pharmaceutically acceptable carrier, excipient or other additive, if necessary.
Also provided is a compound of formula (I), as defined above, or a pharmaceutically acceptable salt thereof, for use in the treatment of the human or animal body.

Further, the present invention provides the use of a compound of formula (I), or a pharmaceutically acceptable salt thereof, in the manufacture of a medicament for use in the treatment of acute respiratory distress syndrome, cystic fibrosis, emphysema, chronic bronchitis, coagulation disorders or bacterial infections. The pharmaceutical composition containing a compound of formula (I) or salts thereof may be prepared in a conventional way by employing conventional non- toxic pharmaceutical carriers or diluents in a variety of dosage forms and ways of administration.

In particular, the compounds of formula (I) can be administered: A) orally, for example, as tablets, troches, lozenges, aqueous or oily suspension, dispersible powders or granules, emulsions, hard or soft capsules, or syrups or elixirs. Compositions intended for oral use may be prepared according to any method known in the art for the manufacture of pharmaceutical compositions and such composition may contain one or more agents selected from the group consisting of sweetening agents, flavouring agents, colouring and preserving agents in order to provide elegant and palatable preparations.

Tablets contain the active ingredient in admixture with non-toxic pharmaceutically acceptable excipients which are suitable for the manufacture of tablets. These excipients may be, for example, inert diluents, such as calcium carbonate, sodium carbonate, lactose, calcium phosphate or sodium phosphate; granulating and disintegrating agents, for example maize starch or alginic acid; binding agents, for example maize starch, gelatin or acacia, and lubrificating agents,
for example magnesium stearate or stearic acid or talc. The tablets may be uncoated or they may be coated )y known techniques to delay disintegration and absoφtion in the gastrointestinal tract and thereby provide a sustained action over a longer period. For example, a time delay material such glyceryl monostearate or glyceryl distearate may be employed. Formulations for oral use may also be presented as Jjard gelatin capsules wherein the active ingredient is mixed with an inert solid diluent, for example calcium carbonate, calcium phosphate or kaolin, or soft gelatin capsules wherein the active ingredient is mixed with water or an oil medium, for example peanut oil, liquid paraffin or olive oil. Aqueous suspensions contain the active materials in admixture with excipients suitable for the manufacture of aqueous suspensions. Such excipients are suspending agents, for example, sodium carboxymethylcellulose, methylcellulose, hydroxypropylmethyl cellulose, sodium alginate, polyvinylpyrrolidone, gum tragacanth and gum acacia; dispersing or wetting agents may be naturally-occurring phosphatides, for example lecithin, or condensation products of an alkylene oxide with fatty acids, for example polyoxyethylene stearate, or condensation products of ethylene oxide with long chain aliphatic alcohols, for example heptadecaethyleneoxyacetamol, or condensation products of ethylene oxide with partial esters derived from fatty acids and an hexitol such as polyoxyethylene sorbitol monooleate, or condensation products of ethylene oxide with partial esters derived from fatty acids and a hexitol anhydrides, for example polyoxysorbitan monooleate.

The said aqueous suspension may also contain one or more preservatives, for example ethyl or n-propyl -hydroxybenzoate, one or more colouring agents, one or more flavouring agents, one or more sweetening agents such as sucrose or saccharin. An oily suspension may be formulated by suspending the active ingredient in a vegetable oil, for example arachis oil, olive oil, sesame oil, coconut oil or in a mineral oil such as liquid paraffin. The oily suspension may contain a thickening agent, for example beeswax, hard paraffin or cetyl alcohol. Sweetening agents, such as those set forth above, and flavouring agents may be added to provide a palatable oral preparation.

These compositions may be preserved by the addition of an antioxidant such as ascorbic acid. Dispersible powders and granules suitable for preparation of an
aqueous suspension by the addition of water provide the active ingredient in admixture with a dispersing or wetting agent, a suspending agent and one or more preservatives. Suitable dispersing or wetting agents and suspending agents are exemplified by those already mentioned above. Additional excipients, for example sweetening, flavouring and colouring agents may also be present.
The pharmaceutical compositions of the invention may also be in the form of oil-in-water emulsions.

The oily phase may be a vegetable oil, for example olive oil or arachis oil, or a mineral oil, for example liquid paraffin or mixtures of these. Suitable emulsifying agents may be naturally-occurring gums, for example gum acacia or gum tragacanth, naturally-occurring phosphatides, for example soy bean, lecithin, and esters or partial esters derived from fatty acids and hexitol anhydrides, for example sorbitan monooleate, and condensation products of the said partial esters with ethylene oxide, for example polyoxyethylene sorbitan monooleate. The emulsions may also contain sweetening and flavouring agents. Syrups and elixirs may be formulated with sweetening agents, for example glycerol, sorbitol or sucrose. Such formulations may also contain a demulcent, a preservative, colouring and flavouring agents. B) parenterally, either subcutaneously or intravenously or intramuscularly, or intrasternally, or by infusion techniques. The pharmaceutical compositions may be in the form of a sterile injectable aqueous or olagenous suspensions.

These suspensions may be formulated according to the known art using those suitable dispersing or wetting agents and suspending agents which have been mentioned above. The sterile injectable preparation may also be a sterile injectable solution or suspension in a non-toxic parenterally-acceptable diluent or solvent, for example a solution in 1,3-butanediol. Among the acceptable vehicles and solvents that may be employed are water, Ringer's solution and isotonic sodium chloride solution. In addition, sterile fixed oils are conventionally employed as a solvent or suspending medium. For this purpose any bland fixed oils may be conventionally employed including synthetic mono or diglycerides. In addition fatty acids such as oleic acid find use in the preparation of injectables.
The daily dose varies according to the activity of the specific compound, the age, weight, and conditions of the subject to be treated, the type and the severity of the disease, and the frequency and route of administration. Typically the daily dose is from 0J to 50 mg per kg of body weight. The amount of active ingredient that may be combined with the carrier materials to produce a single dosage forn\-will vary depending upon the host treated and the particular mode of administration. For example, a formulation intended for oral administration may contain from 5 to 95% of the total composition. Dosage unit forms will generally contain between from 5 to 500 mg of the active compound. The Examples which follow further illustrate the present invention.

General Procedures All compounds prepared were racemic unless explicitly indicated.
Melting points (m.p.) were obtained using a Kofler heated-stage microscope. Values are quoted to the nearest 1 °C and are uncorrected for systematic errors.

Flash column chromatography was accomplished using silica gel 60 GB254, using a modification of the procedure of Still (W. C Still et al, J. Org. Chem., 1978, 43, 2923). Thin layer chromatography was performed on Merck silica gel 60 F254 0.2 mm precoated aluminium backed plates, and visualized by the quenching of ultraviolet fluorescence (254 nm), by staining with iodine, or by treatment with ammonium molybdate solution (10% in IM H2SO4 aq.), potassium permanganate (3g KMnO4, 20g K2CO3, 5 ml 5% NaOH, 300 ml H2O), or phosphomolybdic acid (PMA) (230g PMA in 1 gal. 95% EtOH), followed by heating. Retention factors are quoted to the nearest 0.05.

Optical rotations were obtained using a Perkin-Elmer 241 polarimeter at 589 nm (Na D-line) at the temperature specified for each compound, with a path length of 10 cm. Concentrations (c) are quoted in g/100 ml. Fourier Transform Infrared (FT-IR) spectra were recorded as thin films or

KBr discs, using a Perkin-Elmer Paragon 1000 (FT-IR) spectrometer. Only selected absoφtions are reported. Absorptions are reported in wavenumbers (cm"1), using the
following abbreviations; w, weak; m, medium; s, strong; br, broad.

Proton nuclear magnetic resonance ('H NMR) spectra were recorded at 200 and 500 MHz on Varian Gemini 200 or Brucker AC200, and Brucker AM-500 or AMX500 instruments respectively. Chemical shifts (δH) are quoted in parts per million (ppm), relative to tetramethylsilane, and are referenced to the residual protonated solvent peak. Coupling constants (J) are quoted to the nearest 0.5 Hz or 0.1 Hz, on the 200 or 500 MHz machines respectively. The following abbreviations are used to report the spectra: s, singlet; d, doublet; t, triplet; q, quartet; m, multiplet; dd, doublet of doublets; dt, doublet of triplets; br, broad. Carbon nuclear magnetic resonance (13C NMR) spectra were recorded at

50.31 MHz on Varian Gemini 200 spectrometers using Distortionless Enhancement by Polarisation Transfer (DEPT) editing to aid assignment. Chemical shifts (δc) are quoted in ppm and referenced to the appropriate residual deuterated solvent peak.

Low resolution mass spectra irn/z) were recorded using a Micromass Platform machine atmospheric pressure chemical ionisation (APCI) or electrospray. Only molecular ions, and major peaks are reported. Intensities are recorded as percentages relative to the largest peak.

All solvents were distilled before use. Anhydrous THF was obtained by distillation from sodium/benzophenone ketyl under nitrogen. Anhydrous methanol was prepared by the method of Lund and Bjerrum as described in Nogel (A.L Nogel,

Textbook of Practical Organic Chemistry, 4th Edition, Longman, London, 1984). The fraction of light petroleum ether boiling in the range 40-60°C is referred to as PE 40-60. Solvents were evaporated on a Bϋchi Rl 10 Rotavapor, high boiling sovlents being removed on a Bϋchi Rl 10 Rotavapor equipped with dry-ice condenser at <2 mmHg.
